title: Quotations on the Bank of Amsterdam, the VOC, Holland's and England's public debt, the Stop of the Exchequer and the Bank of England (Chapter 15)
source: Smith (1776, third-edition text); Quinn & Roberds (2010); Frost, Shin & Wierts (2020); Gelderblom, de Jong & Jonker (2012); Gelderblom & Jonker (2004, 2011); Temple (1673); North & Weingast (1989); Andréadès (1909); Evelyn ed. Bray (1901); the Bill of Rights (1689); 5 & 6 Will. & Mar. c. 20 (1694) and 12 & 13 Will. III c. 12 (1701) in Statutes of the Realm; Stasavage (2002); Sussman & Yafeh (2006); Quinn (2001); Temin & Voth (2008); Pincus & Robinson (2014)
series: one row per quoted fact: id, dynasty (here: country or city), year (approximate where year_note says so), year_note, value (several values separated by ';'), unit, numeral (unused here), file (a key of sources below), juan (here: page, section or diary date), quote (verbatim), note
license: Short quotations only, for comment and teaching. Smith, Temple, Evelyn, Andréadès and the statutes are in the public domain; the Bill of Rights is Crown copyright under the Open Government Licence; the modern research is quoted, not copied.
notes: Rows citing txt, pdf and html sources are checked against the downloaded documents by verify_web_quotes.py. Rows citing temple1673, andreades1909img and nw1989img were read by eye on the page images listed in each source's version (format image) and are counted but not checked by a script. Transcription: long s is written s; Temple's capitals and spelling are kept. North & Weingast's tables are quoted as their rows read in the text layer (columns separated by spaces). Translations into Chinese in the chapter are the book's own. Two accounts of the Bank of England's subscription differ (North & Weingast: a third on the first day; Luttrell via Andréadès: £300,000 of £1,200,000); the chapter shows both. Temple's 65 million guilders for Holland's debt is about half Gelderblom & Jonker's estimate for the same years (snapshot gj2011_holland_debt); the chapter shows the gap. Andréadès describes the 1701 settlement of the goldsmiths' debt as annuities that were to cease once half the capital was repaid; the Act itself (row st1701_redeem) charges 3 per cent on the principal 'for ever', redeemable on payment of half the principal, and the chapter follows the Act.
